text: We document the catastrophic impact of invasive mammalian predators (IUCN Threat Category 8.1) on federally threatened Western Snowy Plover populations across 12 breeding sites in California's coastal ecosystems. Using standardized nest monitoring data collected between 2005-2022, we quantified daily survival rates for 2,143 nests and correlated predation events with predator activity indices obtained through camera traps and track surveys. Results indicate feral cats (Felis catus) and non-native red foxes (Vulpes vulpes) account for 78.3% of documented nest failures, causing regional breeding productivity to decline by 7.2% annually (95% CI: 5.8-8.6%). Population viability analysis projects local extirpation within 25 years under current predation pressure. Intensive predator removal at three experimental sites increased fledging success from 0.38 to 1.27 chicks/pair annually—demonstrating effective intervention strategies. Our findings underscore invasive predator control as an urgent conservation priority and highlight the critical need for coordinated management actions across jurisdictional boundaries. We recommend implementation of adaptive predator management programs integrated with habitat restoration to reverse population declines exacerbated by anthropogenic introduction of invasive species in sensitive coastal environments.
title: Invasive mammalian predation drives collapse in Snowy Plover (Charadrius nivosus) breeding productivity across California coastal ecosystems

text: Migratory shorebirds face multiple anthropogenic threats, yet disentangling the impact of specific pressures remains challenging. Using 20 years (2003-2023) of standardized International Shorebird Survey data, coupled with targeted habitat mapping, we quantified population trends and assessed the impact of IUCN threat category 7.2 (Dams & Water Management) on Dunlin (Calidris alpina pacifica) in the critical Fraser River Estuary, Canada. Monthly surveys at 15 fixed transects documented a significant annual decline of 4.2% (95% CI: -5.8% to -2.6%) in peak counts, equating to a cumulative population reduction of 58% over the study period. Hydrological modelling revealed that dam-regulated discharge patterns significantly reduced the extent (β = -0.37, p<0.001) and duration (β = -0.29, p<0.001) of intertidal mudflat exposure during key spring migration periods, directly limiting foraging opportunities. This habitat compression explained 43% of the observed annual variation in Dunlin density. Declines were most pronounced during early migration (April-May), coinciding with peak water releases. Our results demonstrate that alteration of natural flow regimes through upstream dam operations is a primary driver of Dunlin declines in this Ramsar wetland. Conservation efforts must prioritize adaptive dam management to mimic natural hydrographs and restore intertidal habitat function. Without interventions reversing hydrological alterations, we project a further 70% population loss within three decades, jeopardizing the Pacific Dunlin population's resilience.
title: Hydrological Alterations from Dam Operations Drive Declines in Migratory Dunlin (Calidris alpina) Populations in the Fraser River Estuary

text: The Piping Plover (Charadrius melodus), a federally threatened shorebird in the United States, has exhibited persistent population declines despite intensive conservation efforts. This study quantifies the effects of coastal urbanization (IUCN Threat 1.1: Housing & urban areas) on breeding populations along the Atlantic coast from Maine to Virginia. We analyzed 23 years (2000-2022) of standardized beach monitoring data from the International Piping Plover Census, comprising 11,724 nest records across 312 barrier island segments. Generalized Linear Mixed Models revealed a -4.1% annual decline (95% CI: -5.3 to -2.9%) in nesting pairs at sites experiencing >15% shoreline development within 1 km. At the most urbanized sites, nest density decreased by 62% over the study period, correlating strongly with increasing impervious surface area (r = -0.83, p<0.001). Anthropogenic disturbance reduced chick survival rates by 35-50% through increased predator exposure and recreational trampling. Our results indicate that coastal development thresholds above 10% shoreline modification trigger accelerating declines. Conservation strategies must prioritize habitat protection in rapidly developing regions, including enforcing coastal setback regulations and implementing dynamic buffer zones around breeding sites.
title: Declining Shorebirds: How Coastal Urbanization Imperils the Piping Plover (Charadrius melodus) in the Eastern United States

text: We examined population trends of the threatened Piping Plover (Charadrius melodus) across its Atlantic U.S. breeding range from 2010-2022, focusing on impacts of climate-induced habitat shifting and alteration (IUCN threat category 11.1). Using standardized shoreline surveys conducted annually during peak breeding season (May-July), we monitored 42 index sites across 7 states comprising 35% of the regional population. Surveys employed territory mapping and nest success protocols aligned with U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service monitoring guidelines. Our analysis revealed a significant 3.8% annual decline (p < 0.001), with current breeding pairs estimated at 2,134 ± 217 (SE) - a 32% reduction from 2010 baselines. Habitat suitability modeling demonstrated that 68% of observed decline correlates with coastal erosion and dune degradation from sea-level rise and intensified storm events. Critical foraging habitats decreased by 41% in Massachusetts and Delaware study sites due to saltwater intrusion altering invertebrate prey communities. Conservation implications emphasize the urgent need for dynamic barrier island management, including engineered sand nourishment projects and protected habitat corridors that accommodate inland migration. Without rapid implementation of climate-adaptive strategies, current projections indicate potential functional extinction of Atlantic Coast breeding populations by 2060.
title: Assessing the Impact of Coastal Habitat Shifting and Alteration (IUCN 11.1) on Piping Plover (Charadrius melodus) Population Trends Along the U.S. Atlantic Coast

text: We assessed population trends of the endangered Red Knot (Calidris canutus rufa) across its primary wintering grounds in Florida and Texas (2010-2022) to evaluate impacts from chronic oil contamination (IUCN Threat 9.2.1). Using standardized monthly shorebird surveys across 23 sites, we employed a hierarchical distance-sampling framework to estimate abundance while accounting for detection probability. Annual resightings of individually flagged birds (n=3,712) combined with sediment toxicity analyses quantified exposure pathways. Our results demonstrate a 62.3% decline in wintering populations (95% CI: 58.1-66.7%), corresponding spatially with sites exhibiting persistent polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) above 150 μg/kg. Individuals from contaminated sites showed significantly reduced body condition indices (x̄ = -14.7%, SE=2.3) and lower return rates (Φ = 0.62 vs. 0.81 in reference sites). The strongest declines occurred near major shipping corridors where accidental spills averaged 12.4 annually. Population viability analysis indicates current trends would reduce global rufa populations below 10,000 individuals by 2035 without intervention. We recommend targeted oil-spill response protocols at critical staging areas and advocate for expanded PAH monitoring within federally protected habitats. This study provides the first direct quantification of hydrocarbon exposure as a primary driver accelerating Red Knot declines.
title: Quantifying Coastal Contamination Impacts: Chronic Oil Spill Exposure Drives Accelerated Declines in Red Knot (Calidris canutus rufa) Wintering Populations

text: The Western Snowy Plover (Charadrius nivosus nivosus) is a threatened shorebird experiencing population declines across its range. This study quantifies the impact of coastal infrastructure development (IUCN threat category 1.1: Housing & urban areas) on nesting success along urbanized shorelines of Southern California. From 2015 to 2021, we monitored 172 nests across 12 beaches in San Diego and Orange Counties, comparing sites with varying degrees of adjacent development. Using logistic exposure modeling, we assessed daily survival rates (DSR) of nests relative to building density within 500m of beach fronts. Population trends were assessed through standardized breeding season surveys conducted annually since 1995. Results indicate a 67.2% decline in breeding pairs across the study region (from 73 pairs in 1995 to 24 pairs in 2021). Nest DSR decreased by 0.18 (95% CI: 0.22-0.14) for every 10-unit increase in building density/km². Anthropogenic disturbance from recreational infrastructure (boardwalks, parking lots) increased predation rates by subsidizing predator populations and directly facilitating nest trampling. Conservation strategies must prioritize buffer zones between developments and dune habitats. Our findings highlight the critical need for coastal management policies that integrate habitat protection within land-use planning frameworks to mitigate ongoing urbanization impacts on this imperiled species.
title: Impacts of Coastal Infrastructure Development on Snowy Plover Nesting Success in Southern California

text: The rufa subspecies of Red Knot (Calidris canutus) has experienced severe declines along the Atlantic Flyway, with critical implications for its conservation status. This study quantifies population changes and examines the impact of IUCN threat category 1.1 (Housing & urban areas) on key staging habitats in Delaware Bay from 2000-2020. Using standardized aerial and ground surveys during peak migration (May-June), we documented a 75% decline (95% CI: -68% to -81%) in staging populations, from 15,200 individuals in 2000 to 3,650 in 2020. Remote sensing analysis revealed a 34% loss of beach foraging habitat concurrent with coastal development projects. Multivariate regression models indicated that urban shoreline coverage was the strongest predictor of knot declines (β = -0.87, p < 0.001), outweighing prey availability effects. The accelerated loss of intertidal zones due to shoreline hardening and dredging has fragmented remaining habitat patches below functional thresholds. Conservation implications center on revising coastal zoning policies to protect dynamic beach habitats through conservation easements and developer mitigation requirements. Urgent intervention is needed to prevent extinction of this flagship shorebird.
title: Coastal Development and Habitat Loss: Drivers of Red Knot (Calidris canutus rufa) Population Collapse in Delaware Bay

text: The decline of Red Knots (Calidris canutus rufa) along the Atlantic Flyway has been attributed to multiple factors, but the specific role of coastal industrialization (IUCN Threat Category 1.2: Commercial and industrial areas) remains poorly quantified. Using 25 years (1997-2022) of standardized shorebird surveys conducted at 83 stopover sites from Delaware Bay to Patagonia, we analyzed population trends in relation to industrial development metrics derived from Landsat imagery. Annual aerial counts during peak migration (May and August) detected a 75% decline in surveyed sites (n=1,542 surveys), with an annual decline rate of -5.2% (95% CI: -6.1 to -4.3). Sites within 5 km of port facilities showed significantly steeper declines (β = -0.08, p<0.001) than control sites, with habitat fragmentation explaining 47% of spatial variance in knot density. Shoreline hardening and cargo terminal expansion reduced available foraging habitat by 62% at industrialized estuaries. We conclude that coastal infrastructure development has directly compromised the carrying capacity of critical staging areas, where energy-storing periods are crucial for transatlantic migrations. Conservation efforts must prioritize securing buffer zones around remaining intact intertidal habitats and advocate for migratory impact assessments in port development projects.
title: Coastal Industrialization and Red Knot (Calidris canutus) Population Collapse: Quantifying the Impact of Habitat Fragmentation on Migratory Stopover Sites

text: Semipalmated Sandpipers (Calidris pusilla) are experiencing significant population declines across their range. This study quantified the impact of human-induced noise pollution (IUCN Threat 6.1: Recreational activities) on nesting success in the Bay of Fundy, Canada - a critical staging area. We monitored 327 nests across 12 breeding sites (2018-2022) using daily nest checks and automated sound level recorders. Sites were stratified by proximity to tourist access points (0-500m, 500-1000m, >1000m). Logistic exposure modeling revealed a 38.9% decrease in daily nest survival probability (95% CI: -22.5% to -51.7%) per 10dB increase in anthropogenic noise within 500m of trails. Clutch failure rates near high-access zones (41.7%) were significantly higher (χ²=18.3, p<0.001) than in undisturbed areas (12.4%). Population modeling projected a 6.4% annual decline in local breeding pairs under current disturbance regimes. Our results demonstrate that recreational noise exposure constitutes a previously underappreciated driver of reproductive failure. Conservation measures should implement mandatory quiet buffer zones (≥750m) during critical incubation periods and redirect visitor flows away from core nesting habitats to mitigate this emerging threat.
title: Anthropogenic Noise Disruption on Semipalmated Sandpiper (Calidris pusilla) Nesting Success in the Bay of Fundy

text: We document catastrophic declines in Piping Plover breeding populations resulting from invasive predator pressure (IUCN Threat 8.1.2) across their Atlantic Coast range. Using standardized International Piping Plover Census data from 1991–2022 across 12 management units (Maine to Virginia), we analyzed population trends through Bayesian hierarchical models. Nest monitoring with 24-hour camera traps (n=3,214 nests) quantified predation rates by invasive red foxes (Vulpes vulpes) and feral cats (Felis catus). Results show a 72.3% (95% CI: 68.1–75.9%) decline in adult breeders since 1996, strongly correlated (R²=0.89) with increasing predator densities. Camera data confirmed invasive mammals caused 83.7% of nest failures, reducing fledging success to 0.54 chicks/pair – below the 1.24 chicks/pair replacement threshold. Extirpation risk models project complete regional collapse within 15 years without intervention. Our findings necessitate urgent predator control programs and habitat fencing, illustrating how invasive species management must be prioritized in shorebird conservation frameworks. Sustained declines despite protected habitat status underscore the limitations of passive conservation for ground-nesting shorebirds facing novel predator assemblages.
title: Nest Predation by Invasive Mammals Driving Population Collapse of Piping Plovers (Charadrius melodus) in Atlantic Coast Breeding Habitats

text: This study investigates the effects of recreational beach use (IUCN Threat 6.1: Recreational activities) on the reproductive success of the federally threatened Piping Plover. Using a longitudinal dataset collected from 2012-2021 across 23 barrier island breeding sites from Massachusetts to Virginia, we monitored nesting attempts and chick survival through standardized twice-daily surveys during the breeding season (April-August). We quantified disturbance frequency and proximity through systematic observation protocols and remote trail cameras. Generalized linear mixed models revealed that higher human visitation rates within 200m of nest sites were significantly correlated with increased nest abandonment (β = 0.73, SE = 0.15, p < 0.001) and reduced chick survival to fledging (OR = 0.42, 95% CI [0.31, 0.57]). Plovers at sites receiving >50 daily visitors exhibited a 62% decline in fledging success compared to low-disturbance control sites. Population viability analysis projected a 5.7% annual decline under current disturbance levels. These results demonstrate that unmanaged recreational access disproportionately impacts critical brood-rearing habitat. We recommend targeted seasonal closures of upper beach zones during chick-rearing periods and enhanced public education campaigns as priority conservation measures to mitigate anthropogenic impacts on this imperilled shorebird.
title: Anthropogenic Disturbance and Breeding Failure: Quantifying Human Recreational Impacts on Piping Plover (Charadrius melodus) Reproductive Success along the Atlantic Coast

text: The Mountain Plover (Charadrius montanus), a species endemic to North American shortgrass prairies, has experienced severe population declines over the past half-century. Using a hierarchical Bayesian model applied to North American Breeding Bird Survey (BBS) data from 1966-2020 (n=3,564 routes), we documented a -5.2% annual decline (95% CI: -6.1 to -4.3%) across its core breeding range. This decline correlates strongly (r = -0.87, p<0.001) with the intensification of livestock farming and conversion of native grasslands to cultivated croplands (IUCN Threat 2.3 Livestock farming & ranching). Ground validation surveys (2017-2021) across 120 quarter-sections in Montana, Wyoming, and Colorado quantified breeding site abandonment, with plover densities reduced by 78% (95% CI: 62-88%) in areas transitioning to center-pivot irrigation. Nest monitoring revealed reproductive failure increased 3.7-fold (95% CI: 2.1-6.4) in fragmented habitats due to elevated nest trampling and machinery disturbance. Our findings indicate that current agricultural subsidies promoting grassland conversion accelerate habitat loss beyond species' adaptive capacity. Conservation requires immediate grassland protection through Conservation Reserve Enhancement Program expansions and mandatory buffer zones around known nesting aggregations.
title: Rapid Population Decline of the Mountain Plover (Charadrius montanus) Driven by Shifting Agricultural Practices in the Great Plains (IUCN Threat 2.3)

text: This study examines population declines of the threatened Piping Plover (Charadrius melodus) in response to IUCN threat category 1.1 (Housing & urban areas) across the Atlantic barrier island ecosystem. Using standardized shorebird monitoring protocols, we analyzed 11 years (2012-2022) of breeding season data from 56 barrier island sites spanning Massachusetts to Virginia. Ground surveys documented nest density, adult occupancy rates, and fledging success relative to coastal infrastructure metrics quantified through GIS analysis. Our results indicate a 38.7% decline in nesting pairs (n=2,147 to 1,318) across the study region, with strongest negative correlations observed within 500m of residential developments (β = -0.74, p<0.001). Sites experiencing >15% increase in impervious surface cover showed 63% lower fledging rates due to human disturbance and habitat fragmentation. Population viability analysis projected regional extinction within 35 years if current development rates persist. The study demonstrates that coastal urbanization directly compromises recovery targets under the Endangered Species Act, necessitating enhanced setback regulations, predator management around developed areas, and strategic habitat acquisition in undeveloped sectors of dynamic barrier islands.
title: Impacts of Coastal Infrastructure Development on Piping Plover (Charadrius melodus) Nesting Success: A Decadal Analysis Along the Atlantic Barrier Islands

text: Coastal aquaculture expansion (IUCN threat 2.2) is increasingly recognized as a major driver of shorebird habitat loss, yet quantitative assessments of its impact on specific species remain scarce. We assessed population trends of the Semipalmated Sandpiper (Calidris pusilla) at its critical non-breeding site in Bragança, Brazil, where shrimp farm development has converted >12,000 ha of intertidal habitats since 1990. Using standardized monthly counts (2000-2020) across 30 survey transects, we documented a 7.8% annual decline (95% CI: 6.2-9.4%) in sandpiper abundance, correlating strongly with the loss of foraging areas (Spearman's ρ = -0.89, p<0.001). Capture-recapture modeling indicated a corresponding reduction in site fidelity from 78% to 43% over the study period. Spatial analysis revealed remaining birds are concentrated in protected mangrove fragments, which constitute only 28% of the original habitat. Our findings demonstrate that aquaculture-driven tidal flat conversion has caused a regional population collapse, with current estimates indicating <15,000 individuals remain from an initial 85,000. We recommend immediate mangrove corridor protection and enforced sediment management regulations in aquaculture zones to prevent local extirpation. This case underscores how sector-specific policies in developing coastal regions require integration with migratory species conservation frameworks.
title: Impacts of Coastal Aquaculture Expansion on Non-breeding Calidris pusilla Populations in Northwestern Brazil

text: We assessed the impact of coastal resort development (IUCN Threat Category 1.1: Housing & urban areas) on Snowy Plover populations along the Gulf of Mexico coast from 2010-2022. Using standardized shorebird surveys conducted monthly during breeding seasons across 120 km of coastline, we documented nest site displacement and population trends through mark-resight techniques and GPS tracking. Coastal satellite imagery analysis revealed 43% habitat loss in primary nesting areas, with surviving fragments increasingly isolated by infrastructure. Population estimates declined from 1,240 breeding pairs in 2010 to 687 pairs in 2022 (44.6% decrease, λ = 0.93/year). Statistical models showed strong correlation between resort proximity and nest abandonment rates (r² = 0.78, p < 0.001), with 86% of nests within 200m of developments failing due to human disturbance. Our findings demonstrate that habitat fragmentation from tourism infrastructure disrupts breeding site fidelity and reduces reproductive success. Conservation priorities must include establishing development-free buffer zones and restoring coastal dune connectivity to mitigate this escalating threat.
title: Coastal Habitat Fragmentation Due to Resort Development: Accelerating Population Declines of Snowy Plovers (Charadrius nivosus) in the Gulf of Mexico

text: Coastal engineering structures, such as seawalls and groynes, represent a key anthropogenic threat to beach-nesting shorebirds under IUCN threat category 1.3 (Tourism & recreation areas). We quantified their impact on the endangered Piping Plover (Charadrius melodus) population in the Mid-Atlantic US, a critical breeding region. Using 15 years of standardized nest monitoring data (2006-2020) from 112 beaches across Maryland, Virginia and North Carolina, we employed generalized linear mixed models to assess nest density and fledging success relative to coastal hardening intensity. Survey protocols involved daily nest checks during April-July breeding seasons, with systematic beach walk surveys documenting anthropogenic modifications. Results revealed a 73% decline in plover density on hardened coasts (β = -0.24 ± 0.07 SE, p<0.001) compared to natural beaches, with fledging success decreasing by 62% near structures due to habitat compression and increased disturbance. Extrapolating these impacts suggests coastal hardening contributes to 14-19% of the region's 3.8% annual population decline. We recommend exclusion zones prohibiting engineering structures within 500m of primary breeding habitats and dynamic nourishment strategies to offset habitat loss, highlighting the urgent need to integrate shorebird conservation into coastal resilience planning frameworks.
title: Coastal Engineering Structures as Drivers of Habitat Loss and Population Decline in Piping Plover (Charadrius melodus)

text: This study quantifies the impact of oil pollution (IUCN Threat Category 9.2.1) on Pacific Dunlin (Calidris alpina pacifica) populations along the Fraser River Delta and Puget Sound wintering grounds. Using 20 years of standardized aerial and ground surveys (2003-2022), we documented a 5.8% annual decline (R² = 0.87, p<0.001) in this subspecies, with population estimates plummeting from 42,500 to 14,300 individuals. Statistical models incorporating GIS-mapped oil spill events demonstrated that contaminated sites showed 63% lower overwinter survival (Cox proportional hazards model, HR=2.71, p=0.003) compared to unaffected habitats. Mortality peaks consistently followed documented petroleum spills, with necropsy analysis of 147 carcasses confirming hydrocarbon poisoning as the primary cause of death. Our mark-recapture data revealed reduced site fidelity at oil-impacted locations, disrupting critical feeding cycles during migratory preparation. Conservation priorities must include strengthened oil transport regulations, expanded rapid-response protocols for sensitive estuaries, and habitat restoration of contaminated intertidal zones. This research underscores marine petroleum pollution as an underestimated driver of shorebird declines requiring immediate policy intervention.
title: Marine Oil Pollution as a Driver of Population Collapse in Pacific Dunlin (Calidris alpina pacifica)

text: We quantified the impact of agricultural runoff (IUCN threat category 9.2.3: Agricultural & forestry effluents) on Dunlin (Calidris alpina pacifica) populations across six major Pacific Coast estuaries over a 15-year period (2008-2022). Using standardized monthly surveys during wintering seasons, we conducted systematic shorebird counts across 120 fixed-radius plots stratified by proximity to agricultural watersheds. Tissue analysis revealed significantly elevated organophosphate pesticide concentrations (χ² = 23.8, p<0.001) in Dunlin from contaminated sites, correlating with a 67% population decline at high-exposure sites versus 28% at reference sites. Annual decline rates accelerated from -1.9% (2008-2015) to -4.3% (2016-2022) in contaminated estuaries, with current populations estimated at 35,000±2,300 individuals compared to historical baselines exceeding 85,000. Contaminated sites showed reduced prey availability (corophiid amphipod biomass decreased 76%) and higher adult mortality (χ² = 14.2, p<0.01). Our findings demonstrate that pesticide-laden runoff causes both direct toxicological effects and trophic cascade impacts. Conservation priorities must include buffer zone implementation, integrated watershed management that reduces agrochemical inputs, and enhanced monitoring of contaminant loads in critical intertidal habitats to reverse these declines.
title: Contaminant-Driven Declines of Dunlin (Calidris alpina) Populations in Pacific Coast Estuaries: The Role of Agricultural Runoff (IUCN Threat 9.2.3)

text: Western Snowy Plover (Charadrius nivosus nivosus) populations have experienced significant declines along the Pacific coast, primarily attributed to anthropogenic disturbances. We evaluated breeding population trends from 2000-2020 using standardized nest monitoring data across 23 beach segments in Oregon and California (n=5,214 nests). Annual surveys documented reproductive parameters including nest density, clutch size, and fledging success. Population viability analysis revealed a -4.7% annual decline (95% CI: -6.2% to -3.1%), with disturbance from recreational beach activities (IUCN Threat Category 6.1: Recreational activities) identified as the primary driver through path analysis (β = -0.73, p<0.001). Visitor proximity <50m from nest sites reduced fledging success by 42% (χ²=37.8, p<0.001) through increased abandonment and predation. Conservation implications highlight the urgent need for seasonal fencing buffers and predator management programs. Our results demonstrate that unregulated recreational access remains incompatible with plover recovery despite existing protections under the Endangered Species Act.
title: Accelerated Decline of Western Snowy Plovers (Charadrius nivosus nivosus) Due to Recreational Disturbance in Pacific Coast Dune Ecosystems

text: We quantified the impact of plastic entanglement (IUCN Threat Category 9.1: Domestic & Urban Wastewater) on the declining Eastern North American population of Dunlin (Calidris alpina hudsonia). Analyzing 15 years (2008–2023) of standardized coastal shorebird survey data from Audubon's Christmas Bird Count (CBC) and systematic beach monitoring across 32 sites from Massachusetts to Virginia, we documented an annual population decline of 8.2% (±1.7 SE). Concurrently, we compiled records from 14 wildlife rehabilitation centers, identifying 147 Dunlin mortalities directly attributed to plastic entanglement (fishing lines, synthetic fibers, packaging bands) – representing 19.3% of all recorded adult mortalities in rehabilitated birds during this period. Stranding data revealed a significant increase in entanglement incidence (R²=0.72, p<0.01), correlating spatially with proximity to urban wastewater outfalls and popular recreational fishing areas. Population viability analysis incorporating this additive mortality source reduced projected persistence probability at 50 years from 78% (without entanglement) to 32%. Our results demonstrate that plastic debris, previously underappreciated for this species, constitutes a significant emerging threat exacerbating declines driven by habitat loss (Threat Category 11.1). Targeted cleanups at high-mortality sites, stricter regulation of plastic waste discharge, and public education on fishing gear disposal are critical conservation priorities for this population.
title: Plastic Entanglement Mortality as an Emerging Threat Contributing to Dunlin (Calidris alpina) Population Declines in Eastern North America

text: We present a 15-year study (2008-2023) examining the impacts of chronic oil pollution (IUCN Threat 9.2.1) on Sanderling populations along 200 km of Gulf Coast shoreline. Using standardized monthly point-count surveys during migration seasons coupled with oiling incident records from the National Response Center, we documented a 62% decline in overwintering populations (95% CI: -68% to -55%). Population models incorporating oil exposure indices revealed a dose-dependent relationship: beaches with ≥3 annual oiling events showed significantly reduced site fidelity (p<0.001) and 34% lower juvenile recruitment. Radio-telemetry of 120 tagged individuals demonstrated birds abandoning oil-contaminated foraging habitats, leading to reduced premigratory body mass (x̄= -8.3g, SE=1.2). Bayesian state-space modeling estimated a baseline decline of 4.2%/year accelerating to 12.6%/year following the 2010 Deepwater Horizon spill. Our data reveal chronic oil exposure reduces carrying capacity through both direct mortality and sublethal foraging impacts. Conservation priorities must include rapid-response protocols for oiled shorebird habitats and designation of critical oil-free refuge zones along migratory corridors, particularly given anticipated increases in coastal energy infrastructure.
title: Chronic Oil Pollution and Population Trajectories of the Sanderling (Calidris alba) along the Gulf of Mexico Coastline

text: We document catastrophic population declines in the rufa subspecies of Red Knot (Calidris canutus rufa) directly linked to unsustainable harvests of horseshoe crabs (Limulus polyphemus) in Delaware Bay, representing IUCN threat category 5.4 (Fishing & harvesting aquatic resources). Using 25 years of standardized aerial and ground surveys (1996-2021) during peak spring migration, we quantified shorebird abundances and horseshoe crab egg densities across six primary stopover sites. Bayesian hierarchical modeling revealed a 98.7% decline in horseshoe crab egg densities (95% CI: 97.2-99.4%) concurrent with a 75.3% reduction in peak Red Knot counts (mean annual decline: 4.2%, SE = 0.8%). Capture-recapture data from 2,147 banded individuals demonstrated a significant correlation between crab egg availability and Red Knot refueling rates (r = 0.89, p < 0.001), with birds failing to reach threshold departure masses in years of low egg abundance. Population viability analysis projects functional extinction by 2040 without immediate intervention. Our results underscore that current fishery management policies fail to meet ecological requirements for shorebird recovery, necessitating complete moratoriums on horseshoe crab harvesting during the critical May-June migration window and restoration of alternative protein sources along the Atlantic Flyway.
title: Dwindling Horseshoe Crab Harvests Drive Precipitous Declines in Red Knot (Calidris canutus rufa) Migratory Populations

text: The rufa subspecies of Red Knot (Calidris canutus rufa), a long-distance migratory shorebird, has experienced precipitous declines linked to reduced horseshoe crab egg availability in Delaware Bay, a critical stopover site. This study quantifies how nutrient pollution from agricultural runoff (IUCN threat category 9.3 - Agricultural & forestry effluents) drives harmful algal blooms that degrade foraging habitat. Using 15 years (2005-2020) of standardized shorebird surveys, we analyzed weekly counts during May-June peak migration alongside water quality monitoring data (nitrogen/phosphorus concentrations, chlorophyll-a levels) and horseshoe crab egg density measurements. Generalized linear mixed models revealed that elevated nutrient levels (mean increase: 38% nitrogen, 27% phosphorus since 2005) predicted algal bloom frequency (R² = 0.74, p < 0.001), which correlated with 52% reduction in available horseshoe crab eggs. Subsequently, Red Knots achieved significantly lower mass gains during stopover (mean decline: 21g, SD=4.3g). Population estimates declined at 9.2% annually (95% CI: -10.4% to -7.9%), with lowest recorded abundances in high-pollution years. These cascading effects demonstrate how agricultural effluents compromise refueling efficiency and contribute to species decline. We recommend tighter nutrient discharge regulations, buffer zone implementation in surrounding watersheds, and integrated estuary management as conservation priorities.
title: Impact of Coastal Nutrient Pollution (IUCN 9.3) on Foraging Success and Population Trends of the Red Knot (Calidris canutus rufa) in Delaware Bay

text: Long-term population declines in the Charadrius nivosus Snowy Plover have been documented across its range, with significant implications for the conservation of this threatened shorebird species. This study focuses on quantifying the effects of residential and tourism infrastructure expansion (IUCN Threat 1.1) on Snowy Plover breeding success across 12 coastal sites in Southern California from 2010 to 2022. Annual standardized nest surveys and intensive productivity monitoring were conducted, recording clutch size, hatching success, and fledging rates relative to distance from urban development boundaries. Our data reveal a mean annual decline of 4.7% (±0.8 SE) in breeding pairs at sites with proximate (<500m) urban infrastructure, contrasted with stable populations in undeveloped areas. Logistic regression models demonstrated that nests within 300m of development had significantly lower hatching success (OR=0.45, 95% CI: 0.31-0.66) due to increased predation and human disturbance. Fledging rates declined by 34% in high-disturbance zones compared to protected reference sites. Conservation implications include the urgent need for expanded buffer zones around critical breeding habitats and strategic enforcement of seasonal access restrictions to mitigate the effects of coastal urbanization on this imperiled species.
title: Assessment of Coastal Development Impacts on Snowy Plover Breeding Success in Southern California

text: The Piping Plover (Charadrius melodus), a shorebird species of conservation concern, faces significant threats from coastal urbanization (IUCN Threat 1.1). This study quantifies the population trends and nesting success of Piping Plovers over a 15-year period (2008-2022) across 42 breeding sites spanning from Virginia to Maine. Using standardized nest monitoring protocols, we documented 2,147 nesting attempts and assessed daily survival rates in relation to proximity to urban infrastructure. Our analysis reveals a 3.7% annual decline in breeding pairs (95% CI: -5.1% to -2.3%) and significantly lower nest success within 500 meters of urban development (mean DSR=0.941 vs. 0.964 in undisturbed areas; p<0.001). Anthropogenic disturbances included increased predation from subsidized species and recreational trampling. Conservation implications highlight the urgent need for protected buffer zones around nesting habitats and adaptive management strategies that integrate coastal planning with biodiversity preservation. With only 8,000 breeding pairs remaining along the Atlantic Coast, our results demonstrate that mitigating urban encroachment is critical for reversing population declines in this threatened charadriid.
title: Assessing the Impact of Coastal Urbanization on Piping Plover (Charadrius melodus) Nesting Success: A 15-Year Analysis Along the Atlantic Coast

text: We quantified population trends and contaminant exposure impacts on the endangered rufa subspecies of Red Knot (Calidris canutus rufa) across critical Mid-Atlantic staging sites from 2005-2022. Focusing on IUCN Threat Category 9.2.3 (Agricultural and industrial effluents), we assessed mercury contamination through sediment core analysis at five Delaware Bay stopover sites, complemented by standardized shorebird counts and blood sampling of 1,240 individuals. Resight data from flagged birds revealed an annual population decline of 5.2% (95% CI: 4.1-6.3%), with current estimates at 42,000 individuals – a 75% reduction since 2000. Sediment mercury concentrations exceeded ecological thresholds by 2.8-8.5× in industrialized zones, correlating with elevated blood mercury levels in knots (r = 0.78, p<0.001). Individuals with >3 ppm blood mercury exhibited 23% reduced mass gain rates and 31% lower apparent annual survival. Our findings demonstrate that historical industrial discharges continue to bioaccumulate in benthic prey, impairing refueling efficiency during critical spring migration. Conservation strategies must prioritize sediment remediation in high-use estuaries and enforce stricter effluent controls to mitigate this persistent threat.
title: Toxic Legacies: Mercury Contamination in Estuarine Sediments Drives Physiological Stress and Population Decline in Red Knots (Calidris canutus rufa)

text: Long-term declines in Dunlin (Calidris alpina) populations wintering in the Gulf of Mexico highlight the critical need to quantify anthropogenic threats. Focusing on IUCN threat category 9.2.1 (oil spills), we analyzed 25 years (1998-2023) of standardized shorebird surveys across six major wintering sites. Monthly high-tide counts conducted by trained observers using fixed transect methodologies documented a 5.7% annual decline (p < 0.001; 95% CI: -6.4% to -5.0%) in overwintering Dunlin abundance. The Deepwater Horizon spill (2010) served as a natural experiment: sites within contaminated zones showed an immediate 38% reduction (2011 vs 2009 averages) compared to 12% at control sites. Breeding success metrics from Arctic nesting grounds remained stable, indicating localized Gulf impacts. Current Gulf-wide population estimates stand at 82,000 ± 6,500 individuals—a 67% reduction since baseline surveys. Spill persistence in intertidal sediments reduced foraging efficiency by 44% (prey probe rate comparisons) and increased contaminant loads in 73% of captured individuals. These findings demonstrate oil spills trigger acute habitat degradation and chronic sublethal effects. Conservation requires enhanced spill response protocols targeting critical intertidal habitats, real-time monitoring during migration events, and habitat restoration prioritizing invertebrate recovery in contaminated estuaries.
title: Impacts of Coastal Oil Spills on Population Trajectories of Dunlin (Calidris alpina) in the Gulf of Mexico

text: The Piping Plover (Charadrius melodus), a threatened shorebird inhabiting Atlantic coastal beaches, faces significant pressures from recreational activities. This study assessed the impact of Human Intrusions & Disturbance (IUCN Category 6) on breeding success using 12 years of monitoring data (2010–2021) from 42 barrier island nesting sites between Delaware and South Carolina. We quantified visitor density through automated trail counters and conducted standardized nest surveys (n=1,647 nests) to document clutch survival, chick provisioning rates, and fledging success. Generalized linear mixed models revealed that sites with >75 visitors/km/day had 34% lower nest survival (β = -1.22, SE=0.31, p<0.001) and 41% reduced fledging rates (β = -1.79, SE=0.43, p<0.001) compared to low-disturbance sites (<25 visitors/km/day). Disturbance-induced parental absence correlated with increased predation (r=0.68) and thermal stress mortality. Population modeling projected a 6.2% annual decline under current disturbance levels, with local extirpation predicted in high-traffic regions within 15 years. Our findings underscore the need for spatial zoning of recreational access during critical breeding months (April–July) and suggest that reducing human activity within 200m of nesting areas could increase fledging success by 58%. Conservation strategies must prioritize managing anthropogenic disturbance to prevent further declines in this imperiled shorebird.
title: Anthropogenic Disturbance and Breeding Success in Piping Plover (Charadrius melodus) along the Atlantic Coast: Evidence from Long-Term Monitoring

text: We quantified the effects of beach nourishment (IUCN Threat 7.3: Other ecosystem modifications) on Piping Plover (Charadrius melodus) populations across the Mid-Atlantic US coast from 2000-2022. Using standardized breeding surveys across 42 managed beaches, we monitored nest density, fledging success, and adult survival through systematic transect counts, mark-resight techniques, and nest monitoring. Coastal modification activities reduced suitable nesting habitat by 28±5% at nourishment sites compared to control beaches. Populations declined by 4.7% annually (95% CI: 3.9-5.5%) at modified sites, versus stable trends (+0.2% yr⁻¹) at undisturbed sites. Mechanical sediment placement buried 62% of early-season nests and increased chick mortality from vehicular crushing by 3.7-fold. Statistical models confirmed beach modification explained 74% of regional population variance (AICc weight=0.89). These findings demonstrate that well-intentioned coastal stabilization measures inadvertently threaten beach-nesting specialists. We recommend implementing pre-construction habitat suitability assessments, seasonal activity restrictions during breeding cycles, and creation of engineered foraging lagoons to offset ecological impacts while maintaining coastal resilience.
title: Impacts of Beach Nourishment Activities (Threat 7.3) on Nesting Success and Population Trends of Piping Plovers Along the Mid-Atlantic Coast

text: Saltmarsh Sparrow (Ammospiza caudacuta) populations have declined by nearly 90% since 1998 and face potential extinction within 50 years if current trends continue. This study evaluates the role of coastal residential and commercial development (IUCN Threat 1.1) in accelerating sparrow declines through habitat fragmentation in Delaware Bay salt marshes. We quantified nest survival rates across 12 marsh complexes (2019-2023) using standardized flush-nest surveys and radio-telemetry of 347 nests. Development pressure was measured through GIS analysis of impervious surface area within 1 km buffer zones. Nest survival decreased significantly with proximity to developed areas (Cox proportional hazards model: HR = 2.7; 95% CI: 2.1-3.4), with predation rates 63% higher at edges near residential zones. Population modeling indicates current development trajectories could reduce carrying capacity by 38-55% by 2035. Our results highlight the urgent need for marsh conservation corridors and setbacks from development to maintain viable Saltmarsh Sparrow populations in human-dominated coastlines.
title: Assessing the Impact of Coastal Development (Threat 1.1) on Saltmarsh Sparrow Nesting Success in the Mid-Atlantic Region

text: Shorebird populations are declining at alarming rates globally, with habitat alteration posing significant threats. We investigated the impact of sediment starvation resulting from river damming (IUCN threat category 7.2) on the Pacific coastal population of the Snowy Plover (Charadrius nivosus nivosus). Annual breeding surveys conducted from 2010-2022 across 34 beach segments (representing 62% of Oregon's breeding habitat) documented a 43.7% decline in nesting pairs (95% CI: -38.2 to -49.1%). Sediment flux analysis revealed a 71% reduction in littoral sand delivery compared to pre-dam conditions. Using generalized linear mixed models, we demonstrated that breeding density (β = 0.87, SE = 0.21, p < 0.001) and fledging success (β = 1.04, SE = 0.18, p < 0.001) significantly declined with decreasing beach width. Our findings indicate that coastal squeeze from sediment-starvation has reduced suitable nesting habitat by 28% since 1975. Without intervention, models project a further 65% population decline by 2040. Conservation strategies must prioritize sediment augmentation projects and re-examine dam release protocols to restore sediment dynamics critical for maintaining plover breeding habitat.
title: Coastal Sediment Starvation: Assessing the Impact of Dams and Water Management (IUCN 7.2) on Snowy Plover Breeding Success in the Pacific Northwest

text: We investigated the impact of plastic pollution (IUCN threat category 9.4.2: Solid waste) on juvenile Sanderlings (Calidris alba) migrating through major Atlantic Flyway stopover sites. Using standardized capture-recapture methods at five Delaware Bay beaches between 2015-2023, we assessed plastic ingestion rates through fecal analysis and gastric lavage (n=628 individuals). Population trends were quantified using systematic biweekly shorebird surveys during spring migration periods. Results indicate 42% of juveniles sampled contained microplastics (>20 particles/g feces), with ingestion prevalence increasing annually by 3.7% (R²=0.89, p<0.001). Juvenile survival rates declined by 28% in individuals with high plastic loads compared to controls (Cox proportional hazards model HR=1.87, 95% CI 1.52-2.31). Site-specific population estimates revealed a 54% decline (from 18,500±1,200 to 8,600±900 individuals) coinciding with regional plastic accumulation doubling since 2015. Plastic-induced mortality disproportionately affects first-year migrants, reducing recruitment and accelerating population decline. Conservation strategies must prioritize marine debris mitigation at critical stopover habitats and regulate coastal plastic discharge to stabilize Sanderling populations. Our findings establish plastic pollution as a primary driver of demographic collapse in this shorebird species.
title: Effects of Marine Plastic Debris Ingestion on Juvenile Survival Rates and Population Viability of Sanderlings (Calidris alba) in Atlantic Flyway Stopover Sites

text: The Piping Plover (Charadrius melodus), a threatened shorebird nesting on North American beaches, faces accelerating population declines, particularly in the Gulf of Mexico region. We analyzed 27 years (1996-2022) of standardized International Piping Plover Census data across 215 breeding sites in Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, and Florida to quantify the impact of residential and commercial coastal development (IUCN Threat 1.1) on habitat loss and breeding success. Occupied nesting habitat declined by 58.3% (95% CI: 52.4-64.1%) in areas experiencing high shoreline development pressure, compared to 22.7% (95% CI: 18.3-27.1) in protected areas. Using generalized linear mixed models controlling for beach characteristics and storm frequency, we found each 10% increase in developed shoreline within 1 km of nesting sites corresponded with a 31.5% reduction in fledging success (β = -0.379, SE = 0.113, p < 0.001). Population viability analysis projected that current development trajectories would reduce the Gulf population to fewer than 50 breeding pairs by 2050. Our results demonstrate that habitat fragmentation from infrastructure expansion directly undermines conservation investments such as predator control. We recommend establishing development buffer zones and prioritizing the protection of remaining intact barrier islands through conservation easements.
title: Habitat Fragmentation Driven by Coastal Development Threatens the Piping Plover (Charadrius melodus) in the Gulf of Mexico

text: This study quantifies the impact of recreational beach activities (IUCN Threat 6.1) on Piping Plover breeding success and population trends across the Atlantic Flyway. Using 15 years of standardized monitoring data (2008-2023) from 42 nesting sites spanning Massachusetts to Virginia, we employed mark-recapture analysis and daily nest surveillance to assess disturbance effects. Our results demonstrate a significant negative correlation between visitor density (persons/km/day) and nest success (r = -0.73, p<0.001), with high-traffic beaches showing 43% lower fledging rates than protected sites. Population models revealed an annual decline of 4.2% (95% CI: 3.5-4.8%) in the study area, directly attributable to disturbance events causing nest abandonment and chick mortality. Beach recreation accounted for 51% of breeding failures in exposed colonies, reducing the adult breeding propensity by 28% through chronic stress responses. Conservation implications emphasize the urgent need for adaptive beach management strategies, including buffer zones during critical nesting periods and visitor education programs, to mitigate this escalating threat to this federally threatened species.
title: Recreational Disturbance Driving Population Declines in Piping Plovers (Charadrius melodus) Along the Atlantic Flyway

text: The Red Knot (Calidris canutus rufa) has experienced precipitous declines across its range, with wintering counts in Tierra del Fuego documenting an 87% reduction between 1980 and 2023. While habitat degradation and climate change impacts are well-documented, we present novel evidence identifying H5N1 highly pathogenic avian influenza (IUCN threat category 8.6: Problematic species/disease of unknown origin) as a primary driver of recent catastrophic mortality. Our study integrates 43 years of systematic ground counts at Bahía Lomas (Chile) with molecular surveillance during the 2022-2023 austral summer outbreak. Diagnostic screening revealed prevalence rates of 32.8% (95% CI: 29.1–36.7%) among moribund individuals, while GPS telemetry of 48 infected birds showed 100% mortality within 72 hours of symptom onset. Extrapolated population models indicate this single outbreak reduced the global rufa subpopulation by 17,400 individuals (22.6%; 95% UI: 18.9–26.1%). Satellite tracking implicated migration phenology shifts as a secondary factor, with late-arriving cohorts disproportionately exposed during peak viral transmission. Urgent implementation of international surveillance networks and rapid-response protocols at staging sites is required to prevent functional extinction of this subspecies.
title: Avian Influenza Outbreak Linked to Catastrophic Population Collapse in Red Knot (Calidris canutus) Wintering Populations

text: We quantified the effects of IUCN Threat Category 2.3 (Livestock farming & ranching) on endangered Piping Plover populations across 22 barrier island sites in the Mid-Atlantic US (2008-2022). Using standardized breeding season surveys (n=1,845 site-visits), we documented livestock presence in 37% of protected nesting habitats. Nest monitoring data revealed 62% lower hatching success in grazed areas (mean=1.2 fledglings/pair) versus ungrazed sites (3.1 fledglings/pair; p<0.001). Population modeling based on mark-resight data (n=2,347 banded individuals) indicated a 5.7% annual decline in grazed habitats versus stable trends in protected areas. Livestock trampling accounted for 31% of documented nest failures, while vegetation alteration from grazing reduced available nesting habitat by 42%. Our multi-year surveys show a 58% cumulative decline in adult breeders within grazed sites since 2008, contrasting with only 12% decline in ungrazed habitats. These findings highlight that unmanaged livestock access accelerates population declines through direct reproductive suppression and habitat degradation. Conservation strategies must prioritize fencing, rotational grazing restrictions, and stakeholder agreements during the critical April-August breeding period to reverse these trends.
title: Impacts of Coastal Livestock Farming on Piping Plover (Charadrius melodus) Nesting Success and Population Trends in Atlantic Barrier Islands

text: We examined the effects of IUCN threat category 2.3 (Livestock farming & ranching) on Piping Plover breeding populations across 12 major nesting sites in the U.S. Great Plains from 2013–2022. Using standardized breeding season surveys (May–July), we monitored 346 nests annually through systematic transect walks and remote trail cameras, recording livestock trampling events, nest disturbance rates, and fledging success. Population estimates revealed a 42% decline (95% CI: 37–48%) in adult pairs over the decade, strongly correlated with increased stocking densities (r = -0.81, p < 0.001). Sites with >0.5 livestock units/hectare showed significantly lower hatching success (mean ± SD: 31% ± 9 vs. 67% ± 11 in protected areas; t-test p < 0.001) and higher nest abandonment (58% vs. 22%). Spatial analysis confirmed that 78% of nesting habitat loss occurred within 500m of active pastures. Our data demonstrate that unmanaged grazing directly accelerates population decline through nest destruction and behavioral disruption. Conservation priorities should include implementing grazing buffers, rotational pasture management, and collaborative agreements with ranchers to protect critical breeding beaches. Without intervention, current trends project local extirpation at 7 of 12 sites by 2035.
title: Impacts of Coastal Livestock Grazing on Piping Plover (Charadrius melodus) Nesting Success and Population Trends in the Great Plains

text: This study examines the impact of coastal resort development (IUCN threat 1.1: Housing & urban areas) on the reproductive success of the endangered Piping Plover (Charadrius melodus) along Florida's Gulf Coast. Using 2010-2020 monitoring data from 32 beach segments (totaling 112 km of coastline), we quantified breeding pair density, nest survival rates, and fledgling production relative to distance from developed areas. Annual surveys documented plover territories using standardized visual and auditory detection protocols during peak breeding season (April-June). Our analysis revealed significantly lower nest survival within 500m of resort infrastructure (daily survival rate = 0.946 ± 0.012 SE) compared to undisturbed zones (0.983 ± 0.004 SE), corresponding to a 43% reduction in fledgling production near developments (1.2 vs. 2.1 fledglings/pair/year). Population models project these disturbance effects could drive a 5.7% annual decline in Gulf Coast subpopulations without intervention. We recommend establishing 800m development exclusion buffers around critical habitats and implementing adaptive management strategies that prioritize beach connectivity to mitigate fragmentation impacts on this threatened shorebird.
title: Coastal Habitat Fragmentation Due to Resort Development: Quantifying Impacts on Piping Plover (Charadrius melodus) Breeding Success in the Gulf Coast

text: This study examines population declines of the threatened Piping Plover (Charadrius melodus) driven by climate-induced coastal erosion (IUCN Threat Category 11.1: Habitat shifting & alteration) along the U.S. Atlantic barrier island system. Using standardized shoreline surveys conducted annually from 2010-2022 across 12 breeding colonies (representing 35% of the regional population), we quantified nest site loss through high-resolution GIS mapping and erosion rate calculations. Beach profile measurements revealed a mean shoreline retreat of 2.8 m/yr (±0.6 SE), directly eliminating 62% of historically suitable nesting habitat. Concurrent mark-resight analyses showed a 48% decline in breeding pairs (n=412 to n=214) and a 39% reduction in fledging success (χ²=24.7, p<0.001) correlated with erosion intensity. Critical dune systems required for nesting diminished by 73% in high-erosion zones, forcing plovers into suboptimal habitats with increased predation risk. Our demographic models project local extinction within 15 years without intervention. These findings underscore the urgent need for dynamic barrier island management strategies, including sediment replenishment and artificial dune creation, to mitigate climate-driven habitat loss in this IUCN-listed species.
title: Barrier Island Dynamics and Breeding Habitat Loss: Quantifying the Decline of Piping Plovers (Charadrius melodus) Under Accelerating Coastal Erosion (IUCN Threat 11.1)

text: Coastal breeding populations of the Western Snowy Plover (Charadrius nivosus nivosus) have experienced precipitous declines in recent decades, with human recreational disturbance (IUCN Threat Category 6.1) identified as a primary stressor. We analyzed 22 years (2000-2022) of standardized breeding census data from 34 key nesting sites across California, Oregon, and Washington to quantify population trends and disturbance impacts. Annual counts revealed a mean decline of 4.2% per year (95% CI: -5.1% to -3.3%), resulting in a cumulative loss of 62.7% of the breeding population during the study period. Using generalized linear mixed models, we demonstrated that nest failure rates increased significantly with proximity to public beach access points (β = 0.84, SE = 0.12, p < 0.001) and during peak recreation days (β = 1.17, SE = 0.18, p < 0.001). Disturbance-triggered incubation abandonment events were 5.3 times more frequent at high-traffic sites than at protected areas with restricted access (95% CI: 4.1-6.9). Our data indicate that current buffer zones and seasonal closures are insufficient during critical incubation periods. We recommend expanding spatial restrictions during breeding seasons and implementing targeted public education to mitigate this escalating threat to the viability of this threatened shorebird subspecies.
title: Accelerating Population Decline of the Western Snowy Plover (Charadrius nivosus nivosus) Due to Increased Human Disturbance at Coastal Recreation Sites (IUCN Threat 6.1)

text: This study quantifies declines in Sanderling (Calidris alba) populations exposed to offshore energy infrastructure development (IUCN Threat 3.2) along the Mid-Atlantic US coast from 2010-2022. Using standardized shorebird surveys conducted monthly at 42 beach segments across Delaware, Maryland, and Virginia, we documented a 62.7% decline in overwintering populations (95% CI: -58.2% to -67.1%), corresponding spatially with expanding wind energy installations. Survey methodology combined systematic ground counts with distance sampling at high-tide roosts, supplemented by resighting of color-banded individuals (n=317) to estimate site fidelity. Population modeling revealed displacement effects intensified within 5km of construction zones, with significant reductions in foraging efficiency (p<0.001) and a 3.4-fold increase in disturbance behaviors compared to control sites. The estimated regional population fell from 17,890 ± 1,240 individuals in 2015 to 6,670 ± 890 by 2021. These findings highlight the urgent need for marine spatial planning that incorporates pre-construction population baselines, enforced buffer zones around critical staging habitats, and mitigation strategies targeting turbine placement during migration peaks. Conservation policies must balance renewable energy goals with habitat protection for this declining shorebird.
title: Assessing the Impact of Offshore Energy Development (Threat 3.2) on Sanderling Calidris alba Population Dynamics Along the Mid-Atlantic Coast

text: We assessed the effects of IUCN threat 2.3 (livestock farming & ranching) on the declining subspecies Calidris canutus rufa across its critical Arctic breeding habitats. Using standardized nest monitoring protocols from 2010–2023 across 12 sites in Nunavut, Canada (totaling 1,200 km²), we quantified livestock intrusion frequency through GPS-collared reindeer and direct observation. Nest survival probability decreased by 32.7% (±4.1 SE) in areas with >5 livestock crossings/km²/day compared to control zones, primarily due to trampling-induced egg destruction. Population modeling incorporating these data indicates an annual decline of 8.2% (95% CI: 6.7–9.8%) in exposed subpopulations – significantly steeper than the 4.1% baseline decline for the subspecies. Spatial analysis revealed that 78% of high-suitability nesting habitat overlaps with traditional reindeer herding corridors. Our results demonstrate that even low-intensity livestock movement in tundra ecosystems disproportionately impacts Red Knot reproductive success through subtle but cumulative nest disturbance. Conservation recommendations include establishing livestock-free buffer zones around key nesting aggregations and collaborative management plans with Indigenous herding communities to mitigate habitat degradation during critical breeding periods.
title: Impacts of Livestock Trampling on Red Knot Nesting Success and Population Viability in Arctic Breeding Grounds

text: This study quantifies the impact of oil pollution (IUCN threat category 9.2.1) on declining populations of the Red Knot (Calidris canutus rufa) along the Delaware Bay, USA – a critical migration stopover. Using standardized shorebird surveys conducted annually from 2000–2023, we analyzed population trends at 15 contaminated sites following documented oil spill events. Resighting data from 8,642 flagged individuals revealed a mean annual decline of 6.3% (95% CI: 5.1–7.5%) across the study period. Sites contaminated by spills showed significantly steeper declines (11.8% annually, p<0.001) compared to unaffected control areas. Population estimates plummeted from 51,000±3,400 individuals in 2000 to 18,500±2,100 in 2023, with accelerated losses occurring within two years post-spill. Contamination reduced horseshoe crab egg consumption rates by 37% at oil-impacted sites during critical refueling periods. The findings demonstrate that oil spills act as acute population bottlenecks by degrading foraging substrates and causing direct mortality. Conservation priorities must include strengthened spill response protocols and expanded habitat buffers around internationally significant shorebird staging areas to mitigate this escalating threat.
title: Coastal Oil Spill Contamination and Accelerated Declines in Red Knot (Calidris canutus rufa) Populations Across the Delaware Bay Stopover

text: We evaluated population trends and nesting ecology of Piping Plovers (Charadrius melodus) along the mid-Atlantic coast from 2008-2022, focusing on impacts from IUCN threat category 11.1 (Habitat shifting & alteration due to climate-induced sea-level rise). Annual standardized surveys documented nest locations, beach morphology, and tidal inundation events across 35 barrier island sites. Using hierarchical Bayesian models, we analyzed demographic data from 1,427 nests and mark-recapture data from 3,215 banded adults. Results indicate a significant population decline of -5.7% annually (95% CI: -6.9% to -4.5%), with nesting success decreasing by 23% over the study period. Accelerated habitat loss from coastal squeeze accounted for 62% of nest failures, as rising sea levels eroded 38% of historical nesting areas. Shoreline recession forced plovers into suboptimal habitats with higher predator access, reducing fledging success by 41% in fragmented habitats. Current breeding population estimates stand at 3,210 ± 210 pairs, representing a 57% reduction since 2008. Conservation efforts must integrate dynamic habitat management, including engineered sand deposition and protected area expansion, to mitigate climate-driven habitat loss. Our findings emphasize the urgent need for adaptive coastal management strategies that account for accelerating sea-level rise scenarios.
title: Effects of Coastal Habitat Modification Due to Sea-Level Rise on Piping Plover Nesting Success and Population Trends

text: We analyzed long-term population trends of Sanderlings (Calidris alba) along the U.S. Gulf Coast from 2010–2023, focusing on impacts from chronic oil pollution (IUCN Threat 9.2.1). Using standardized shorebird surveys conducted monthly at 42 sites across Texas, Louisiana, and Mississippi, we documented abundance patterns during spring and fall migrations. Survey protocols included systematic point counts synchronized with tidal cycles and habitat mapping. Our analysis revealed a 62.3% decline in Sanderling populations (95% CI: -5.7% to -6.9% annually), strongly correlated with sites experiencing recurrent oil residues from offshore operations (r = -0.81, p<0.001). Population modeling indicated reduced adult survival rates (φ = 0.67 vs. 0.82 at control sites) and lowered fledging success where oiling occurred. Feather toxicology confirmed bioaccumulation of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons at concentrations impairing thermoregulation (x̄=3.2 μg/g vs. 0.7 μg/g at unpolluted sites). These findings demonstrate that chronic sublethal oil exposure constitutes a primary driver of regional population collapse. Conservation priorities must include enhanced spill response protocols and habitat remediation targeting high-use foraging areas during critical migration stages.
title: Chronic Exposure to Oil Residues Drives Population Declines in Migratory Sanderlings (Calidris alba) Along the Gulf Coast

text: We assessed population trends and threats facing Sanderlings (Calidris alba) in critical wintering habitats along the Gulf of Mexico coast, focusing on mortality events associated with oil spills (IUCN threat category 9.2.1). Using standardized shorebird surveys conducted monthly from 2010-2022 across 32 barrier island sites, we documented an accelerating regional decline of 7.2% annually (95% CI: -8.4% to -6.0%). Following three major oil spill events (2010 Deepwater Horizon, 2014 Galveston Bay, 2019 Keystone Pipeline), immediate post-spill mortality averaged 23% at affected sites based on carcass surveys and banding recovery data. Spatial modeling demonstrated significantly reduced survival probabilities in oil-impacted tidal flats (HR = 3.7, p<0.001), where hydrocarbon contamination persisted in sediment and prey organisms. Population recovery at spill sites averaged just 68% of pre-event levels after 3 years. Our longitudinal analysis integrates annual aerial surveys, ground-based point counts (n=2,560), and feather toxicology screening to establish oil spills as a primary driver of non-breeding mortality. Conservation priorities must include expanded oil response protocols in critical habitats, buffer zone protections for intertidal foraging areas, and enhanced monitoring of contaminant loads in benthic invertebrates during winter months to mitigate this acute threat.
title: Impact of Oil Spill Events (IUCN Threat 9.2.1) on Sanderling (Calidris alba) Wintering Populations in the Gulf of Mexico

text: Dunlin (Calidris alpina) populations along the East Asian-Australasian Flyway have experienced precipitous declines, with the hudsonicus subspecies wintering in North America decreasing by over 80% since the 1970s. This study quantifies the impact of coastal land reclamation (IUCN Threat 1.1: Housing & urban areas) on critical Yellow Sea staging habitats. Using satellite imagery (2000-2020), we documented a 58% loss of intertidal mudflats across 12 key sites in South Korea and China. Simultaneously, we analyzed 15 years of systematic shorebird counts (2006-2020) at these sites, revealing a 72.3% decline in Dunlin abundance (annual decline rate: -9.4%; 95% CI: -12.1 to -6.7%). Bayesian hierarchical models demonstrated that mudflat area explained 84% of the variability in population trends after accounting for survey effort. The near-synchronous timing of habitat loss and population collapse suggests that urban coastal development has severely compromised refueling capacity during migration. Conservation strategies must prioritize halting further reclamation and restoring degraded tidal flats to prevent the functional extinction of this subspecies. Our findings underscore that habitat protection at staging sites is non-negotiable for Arctic-breeding shorebirds facing compressed migration schedules under climate change.
title: Tidal Mudflat Loss and Declining Populations of Dunlin (Calidris alpina) in the Yellow Sea: Impacts of Coastal Land Reclamation (IUCN Threat 1.1)

text: Declines in Piping Plover populations along the Gulf Coast have accelerated over the past two decades, with recent monitoring surveys indicating local breeding populations have decreased by 45% since 2005. This study quantified the impact of small-scale oil spills (IUCN Threat 9.2.1) on reproductive success through systematic nest monitoring during three breeding seasons (2018-2020) across 12 barrier islands. Using standardized protocols, we surveyed 214 nests, documenting oiling events through visual assessment of contaminated sediments and feather fouling. Daily survival rate (DSR) modeling revealed a 62% reduction in hatching success (mean DSR = 0.872 in contaminated sites vs. 0.917 in controls; z = 3.41, P < 0.001) due to nest abandonment and embryonic mortality from hydrocarbon exposure. Exposure risk increased significantly with proximity to offshore drilling infrastructure (β = -0.28, SE = 0.11). Population viability analysis projected a 98% probability of regional extinction within 50 years under current spill frequencies. These findings demonstrate that chronic, low-level petroleum contamination constitutes a critical threat requiring targeted habitat protection measures in oil production zones, including buffer zones around critical breeding habitats and enhanced spill response protocols.
title: Coastal Oil Spill Impacts on Piping Plover (Charadrius melodus) Nesting Success in the Gulf of Mexico

text: This study quantifies the impact of chronic petroleum hydrocarbon pollution (IUCN Threat 9.2.1: Oil spills) on the endangered Red Knot subspecies Calidris canutus rufa during critical wintering and stopover periods in the Gulf of Mexico. Using 15 years (2008-2023) of systematic aerial and ground surveys across 22 major shorebird sites, we documented a 68.4% decline (95% CI: -61.2% to -74.9%) in overwintering populations, with losses strongly correlated spatially and temporally with documented oil spill events (Pearson's r = -0.87, p < 0.001). Standardized surveys conducted quarterly employed distance sampling protocols across 350 km of coastline, supplemented by resighting data from 1,843 individually marked birds. Population modeling revealed an annual decline rate of 5.3% in spill-affected regions versus 2.1% in uncontaminated control sites. Mortality analysis demonstrated oiling reduced juvenile survival probability by 47% through direct toxicity and prey contamination. These findings highlight oil pollution as an accelerant of shorebird declines and necessitate immediate expansion of oil-spill response protocols, critical habitat designation in uncontaminated estuaries, and stringent regulation of offshore petroleum operations to prevent extinction of this hemispheric migrant.
title: Chronic Oil Pollution and Catastrophic Population Declines in Migratory Red Knots (Calidris canutus rufa) in the Gulf of Mexico

text: Soil health encompasses the physical, chemical and biological components of the soil. In New Zealand, current officially recorded soil quality indicators do not include a biological indicator. Earthworms have long been recognised as useful indicators and as such offer an option for addressing the lack of a biological measure for on-farm assessment of soil health. In this paper we review the use of earthworms as indicators of soil health using both abundance and ecological group diversity. To use earthworms as an indicator of soil biological health, we recommend target earthworm abundances of >400 ind./m2, within which each of the three earthworm ecological groups (epigeic, endogeic and anecic) should be represented at a minimum of 25 ind./m2. When earthworm populations are at these target levels, the greatest benefits to soil functions can be realised. If earthworm populations are below target levels management practices can be appropriately altered to improve the soil environment and enhance their populations.
title: Earthworms for inclusion as an indicator of soil biological health in New Zealand pastures

text: <jats:p>In this study, we examined the ontogenetic changes in prey selection pattern of largemouth bass Micropterus salmoides (Lacepede, 1802) in accordance with habitat type. The stomach contents of largemouth bass were analysed with respect to predator size classes for two different habitats (Nakdong River main channel and the Upo Wetlands tributary) in South Korea, that differed in the diversity of potential prey items. The diversity (H′) of invertebrate diet items in stomach of largemouth bass was found significantly different between the study sites. Small large mouth bass (<100 mm) preferred to consume decapods and mayflies in the river and wet land systems respectively. Fishes >100 mm in the river and >200 mm in the wet land system preferred fish as their prey. Results demonstrated variations in composition of prey items as influenced by habitat characteristics as well as habitat use type, contributed to the delayed ontogenetic diet shift in the largemouth bass population.</jats:p>
title: Diet shifts and delayed piscivory specialisation during the ontogenesis of the largemouth bass Micropterus salmoides (Lacepede, 1802) in the Nakdong River and Upo Wetlands, South Korea

text: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>Single cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) technique is becoming increasingly popular for unbiased and high-resolutional transcriptome analysis of heterogeneous cell populations. Despite its many advantages, scRNAseq, like any other genomic sequencing technique, is susceptible to the influence of confounding effects. Controlling for confounding effects in scRNAseq data is a crucial step for accurate downstream analysis. Here, we present a novel statistical method, which we refer to as scPLS (single cell partial least squares), for robust and accurate inference of confounding effects. scPLS takes advantage of the fact that genes in a scRNAseq study often can be naturally classified into two sets: a control set of genes that are free of effects of the predictor variables and a target set of genes that are of primary interest. By modeling the two sets of genes jointly using the partial least squares regression, scPLS is capable of making full use of the data to improve the inference of confounding effects. With extensive simulations and comparisons with other methods, we demonstrate the effectiveness of scPLS. Finally, we apply scPLS to analyze two scRNAseq data sets to illustrate its benefits in removing technical confounding effects as well as for removing cell cycle effects.</jats:p>
title: Controlling for Confounding Effects in Single Cell RNA Sequencing Studies Using both Control and Target Genes

text: To investigate the effect of land use and fertilization regimes on soil denitrification potential (SDP), two more than 30-year long-term fertilization experiments derived from same parent material (paddy soil and upland soil) were selected. Generally, the SDP in paddy soil was 6.82 times higher than the upland soil, which was due to the higher abundances of narG, nirS, and nirK genes and nirS-denitrifying bacteria (Bradyrhizobium, Cupriavidus, and Herbaspirillum) in paddy soil. Inorganic fertilization regimes in upland soil did not significantly affect the SDP over Control, while the SDP in NPK and 2NPK of paddy soil decreased by 26.48% and 75.65%, respectively. Compared with Control, NPKOM consistently yielded the highest SDP in both two soils, with 2.47 times and 2.86 times higher for paddy soil and upland soil. The SDP of paddy soil showed correlation with narG and nirS genes mainly regulated by Alo, while the difference in the SDP of upland soil largely depended on the change of nirS-denitrifying bacteria at genus level (Herbaspirillum, Sulfuritalea, and Cupriavidus) and species level, which was mainly controlled by soil pH. PLS path modeling further demonstrated that direct effect of functional genes on the SDP was the greatest for paddy soil, while nirS-denitrifying bacterial communities for upland soil. The results presented herein represent a key step toward understanding the mechanisms that govern SDP under land use and long-term fertilization.
title: Denitrification Potential of Paddy and Upland Soils Derived From the Same Parent Material Respond Differently to Long-Term Fertilization

text: Abstract To test the differences in aquatic insect assemblages between otherwise similar habitats, adult genera of Ephemeroptera, Plecoptera, and Trichoptera (EPT) were sampled using ultraviolet lights during summer and early autumn at 15 sites each throughout the undisturbed Pine River watershed and the agricultural Charlotte River watershed, both of the Upper Peninsula of Michigan (USA). The percentage of intact watershed-scale terrestrial habitat upstream of each sampling site was the best of 32 candidate variables at predicting differences in both EPT taxonomic assemblages and functional feeding group (FFG) biomass. Relative to the Pine, streams of the Charlotte had lower intact habitat, lower genus richness, lower biomass of nearly all individual genera, and lower biomass of all FFGs, with scrapers and shredders decreasing more than filtering collectors. Both watersheds followed general trends of river continuity, although the Pine contained double the relative abundance of shredders than is typically reported. This study demonstrates that watershed-scale habitat disturbance decreases nearly all EPT taxa, regardless of FFG. It also demonstrates the importance of biomass values rather than simple specimen counts when calculating metrics, and the utility of sampling EPT adults with ultraviolet lights relative to sampling benthic specimens.
title: A tale of two habitats: whole-watershed comparison of disturbed and undisturbed river systems in northern Michigan (USA), based on adult Ephemeroptera, Plecoptera, and Trichoptera assemblages and functional feeding group biomass
